title: PostgreSQL Performance Tuning: EXPLAIN ANALYZE & Indexing
description: A deep database performance course covering B-Tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, pgvector indexes, reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE execution plans, autovacuum tuning, and PgBouncer.
body: Optimize high-throughput PostgreSQL databases. Master index selection strategies (B-Tree, GIN, BRIN, pgvector), analyze execution plan buffer reads, tune autovacuum parameters, and manage connection pools with PgBouncer.

sections.title: Section 1: Index Selection Strategies & Partial Indexing

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: B-Tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, and Vector Indexes
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: One Index Type Used for Everything

A team creates a default B-Tree index on every column that shows up in a `WHERE` clause — including a JSONB `metadata` column and a full-text `search_vector` column. Query performance barely improves: B-Tree indexes can't efficiently support containment (`@>`) or full-text (`@@`) operators, so PostgreSQL falls back to a sequential scan for those queries anyway, silently wasting the disk space and write overhead of an index that's never actually used.

### Choosing the Right Index Type for the Query Shape

Each index type is a data structure specialized for a specific class of query — picking the wrong one means the planner can't use it at all, no matter how you tune it:

```sql
-- B-Tree (the default): equality and range queries, ORDER BY, sorting
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_at ON orders (created_at DESC);
-- Supports: WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01', ORDER BY created_at DESC

-- GIN (Generalized Inverted Index): full-text search and JSONB containment
CREATE INDEX idx_articles_search ON articles USING GIN (to_tsvector('english', body));
-- Supports: WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ to_tsquery('postgres & indexing')

CREATE INDEX idx_users_metadata ON users USING GIN (metadata jsonb_path_ops);
-- Supports: WHERE metadata @> '{"plan": "enterprise"}'

-- GiST (Generalized Search Tree): geometric data, range types, nearest-neighbor
CREATE INDEX idx_bookings_daterange ON bookings USING GiST (stay_range);
-- Supports: WHERE stay_range && '[2026-06-01, 2026-06-05]'::daterange (overlap detection)

-- BRIN (Block Range Index): huge, naturally-ordered append-only tables
CREATE INDEX idx_events_time_brin ON events USING BRIN (occurred_at);
-- A fraction of the size of a B-Tree on the same column — stores min/max per
-- disk block rather than a full entry per row. Ideal for time-series tables
-- where rows are inserted roughly in occurred_at order and never updated.

-- HNSW / IVFFlat (pgvector): approximate nearest-neighbor search on embeddings
CREATE INDEX idx_document_chunks_embedding ON document_chunks
  USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
-- Supports: ORDER BY embedding <=> query_embedding LIMIT 10 (semantic search)
```

### Index Type Decision Table

| Query pattern | Index type | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `WHERE col = X`, `WHERE col > X`, `ORDER BY col` | B-Tree | Balanced tree gives O(log n) lookup and native ordering |
| `WHERE jsonb_col @> '{...}'`, full-text `@@` | GIN | Inverted index maps each token/key to the rows containing it |
| Range overlap, geometric containment | GiST | Supports arbitrary "nearness"/overlap predicates, not just equality |
| Time-series, append-only, huge tables | BRIN | Stores block-level summaries instead of per-row entries — tiny footprint |
| Vector similarity search (RAG, recommendations) | HNSW (pgvector) | Approximate nearest-neighbor graph, sublinear search over embeddings |

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: An index that doesn't match the operator in your `WHERE` clause is invisible to the query planner — `EXPLAIN` will show a sequential scan regardless of how many B-Tree indexes exist, because none of them support the operator being used. Always match the index type to the actual operator, not just the column.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.2: Partial & Expression Indexing
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: A Full-Table Index for a Query That Only Ever Wants 2% of the Rows

An `articles` table has 2 million rows, but the admin dashboard's most common query only ever looks at `WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED'` — roughly 40,000 rows. A standard B-Tree index on `(published_at, category_id)` indexes all 2 million rows, including 1.96 million that query never touches, bloating the index and slowing down every write that has to maintain it.

### Partial Indexes: Index Only the Rows You Actually Query

```sql
-- Only indexes rows matching the WHERE clause — dramatically smaller than a
-- full-table index, and PostgreSQL can use it ONLY for queries whose WHERE
-- clause provably implies status = 'PUBLISHED'.
CREATE INDEX idx_articles_published_active
ON articles (published_at DESC, category_id)
WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED';
```

### Expression Indexes: Index a Computed Value, Not a Raw Column

A case-insensitive email lookup like `WHERE LOWER(email) = 'user@example.com'` can't use a plain index on `email` — the planner has no way to know `LOWER(email)` and `email` relate without evaluating the function on every row. An **expression index** indexes the function's output directly:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower ON users (LOWER(email));

-- Now this query uses the index instead of a sequential scan:
SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'user@example.com';
```

The same technique works for a computed "is this row eligible" flag used repeatedly across the codebase:

```sql
-- Index a boolean expression combining two columns
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_needs_review
ON orders ((total_amount > 10000 AND payment_method = 'WIRE'))
WHERE status = 'PENDING';
```

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: Partial and expression indexes both trade generality for size and speed — a partial index only helps queries whose `WHERE` clause the planner can prove is a subset of the index's own `WHERE` clause, so keep the predicate simple and match it to your actual hot-path query, not an approximation of it.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.3: Covering Indexes with INCLUDE to Enable Index-Only Scans
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: An Index That Still Requires a Trip to the Table

A query `SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE username = $1` uses an index on `username` to find the matching row quickly — but PostgreSQL still has to fetch the full row from the table's heap to read the `email` column, because `email` isn't part of the index. For a table under heavy concurrent load, that extra heap fetch (called a "heap visit") is real, measurable latency multiplied across millions of queries per day.

### Covering Indexes: Storing Extra Columns in the Index Itself

```sql
-- INCLUDE adds email into the index's leaf pages WITHOUT making it part of
-- the search key (it's not used for lookups/sorting, only returned).
CREATE INDEX idx_users_username_covering
ON users (username) INCLUDE (email, display_name);

-- This query can now be satisfied ENTIRELY from the index — no heap visit:
SELECT email, display_name FROM users WHERE username = 'alice';
```

```text
  Without INCLUDE:                          With INCLUDE (email, display_name):

  Index lookup on username                  Index lookup on username
         │                                          │
         ▼                                          ▼
  Get row's heap (tid) pointer              Read email + display_name
         │                                   DIRECTLY from the index leaf page
         ▼                                          │
  Heap fetch (extra disk/buffer I/O)                ▼
  to read email, display_name               Return — "Index Only Scan"
         │                                   (visible in EXPLAIN output)
         ▼
  Return
```

The `EXPLAIN` output confirms this by showing `Index Only Scan` instead of `Index Scan` — the distinction between the two is exactly whether PostgreSQL needed to touch the underlying table heap at all. Note that an index-only scan still requires the visibility map to confirm the row is visible to the current transaction, which is one more reason routine `VACUUM` (Lesson 2.3) matters.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: `INCLUDE` is worth adding when a query is run extremely frequently and only ever needs a small, stable set of extra columns — it's not a general-purpose optimization, since every included column still adds to the index's size and write overhead.

sections.title: Section 2: Execution Plan Analysis & Connection Pooling

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: Interpreting `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` Plans
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: A Query That's "Using the Index" But Still Slow

A teammate reports a query is slow "even though it has an index." Looking at plain `EXPLAIN` (without `ANALYZE`) shows an index scan and looks fine — but plain `EXPLAIN` only shows the planner's *estimate*, not what actually happened. The real problem only becomes visible with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, which actually runs the query and reports real timings and real disk activity.

### Reading a Real Execution Plan

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.id, o.total_amount, c.name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'PENDING'
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

```text
Limit  (cost=1204.31..1204.36 rows=20 width=48) (actual time=812.44..812.45 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=203 read=8841
  ->  Sort  (cost=1204.31..1229.18 rows=9948 width=48) (actual time=812.43..812.44 rows=20 loops=1)
        Sort Key: o.created_at DESC
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 27kB
        Buffers: shared hit=203 read=8841
        ->  Hash Join  (cost=245.00..987.60 rows=9948 width=48) (actual time=12.10..789.02 rows=9948 loops=1)
              Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
              Buffers: shared hit=203 read=8841
              ->  Seq Scan on orders o  (cost=0.00..610.00 rows=9948 width=24)
                    (actual time=0.02..701.55 rows=9948 loops=1)
                    Filter: (status = 'PENDING'::text)
                    Rows Removed by Filter: 190052
                    Buffers: shared read=8841
              ->  Hash  (cost=180.00..180.00 rows=5200 width=32) (actual time=11.90..11.90 rows=5200 loops=1)
                    ->  Seq Scan on customers c  (cost=0.00..180.00 rows=5200 width=32)
Planning Time: 0.412 ms
Execution Time: 812.61 ms
```

### What This Plan Reveals

| Signal | What it means |
| :--- | :--- |
| `Seq Scan on orders` + `Rows Removed by Filter: 190052` | The planner is reading all ~200,000 rows and discarding 190,052 of them — there is no usable index on `status` |
| `Buffers: shared read=8841` (not `hit`) | 8,841 blocks came from DISK, not from PostgreSQL's shared buffer cache — the working set doesn't fit in memory or is cold |
| `actual time=0.02..701.55` on the Seq Scan | 701ms of the query's 812ms total is spent in this single sequential scan — this is the bottleneck to fix, not the sort or the join |

**The fix**, informed directly by the plan: add a partial index matching the actual filter (from Lesson 1.2):

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending_created ON orders (created_at DESC) WHERE status = 'PENDING';
```

Re-running `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` after adding this index should show `Index Scan using idx_orders_pending_created` with `Buffers: shared hit=...` (no `read`) on subsequent runs, and execution time dropping from ~800ms toward single-digit milliseconds.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: Always read `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` bottom-up: the deepest, most expensive node (here, the `Seq Scan on orders`) is almost always where the real cost lives, even though it appears last in a top-down node listing. `shared hit` vs `shared read` tells you whether you have a memory problem or an indexing problem — read-heavy plans on a query you expect to be fast are the clearest sign of a missing or unusable index.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.2: Connection Pooling with PgBouncer
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: "FATAL: sorry, too many clients already"

Your Go service scales to 40 replicas during a traffic spike, each holding a connection pool of 25 connections — 1,000 total connections against a PostgreSQL instance configured for `max_connections = 200`. New connections start failing with `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`, taking down the service exactly when it needed to scale up.

Each PostgreSQL backend connection is a full OS process consuming real memory (several MB per connection, more under load) — connections don't scale the way in-process goroutines or threads do.

### PgBouncer: A Lightweight Proxy That Multiplexes Connections

```ini
; pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
gg_cms = host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=gg_cms

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt

; transaction pooling: a client connection is only bound to a real
; PostgreSQL backend connection for the duration of a single transaction,
; then released back to the pool — NOT held for the client's whole session.
pool_mode = transaction

max_client_conn = 2000
default_pool_size = 25
min_pool_size = 5
reserve_pool_size = 5
```

```text
  1,000 app connections (40 replicas × 25 each)
              │
              ▼
      ┌───────────────────┐
      │     PgBouncer       │   listens on :6432, presented to the app
      │  (pool_mode =       │   as if it WERE PostgreSQL
      │   transaction)      │
      └─────────┬──────────┘
                │  multiplexed down to a small, fixed pool
                ▼
      ┌───────────────────┐
      │   PostgreSQL        │   default_pool_size = 25 real backend
      │  (max_connections   │   connections serving all 1,000 clients
      │   = 200)            │
      └───────────────────┘
```

**Important caveat with `pool_mode = transaction`**: session-level features that assume a connection is exclusively "yours" for its whole lifetime — `SET` statements outside a transaction, session-level advisory locks, `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, prepared statements created outside the pooled transaction — behave unpredictably, because the next statement might land on a completely different backend connection. Application code must scope any session-dependent behavior to within a single transaction, or avoid it entirely under transaction pooling.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: PgBouncer doesn't increase how many queries PostgreSQL can process concurrently — it increases how many CLIENT connections can be waiting without each one consuming a scarce, expensive backend process. The real fix for genuine query-processing capacity is still indexing and query tuning (Sections 1 and the previous lesson), not just pooling around a slow query.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.3: Autovacuum Tuning to Prevent Table Bloat
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: A Table That Kept Growing Despite Deleting Old Rows

A `sessions` table has a nightly job that deletes expired rows, yet the table's on-disk size keeps climbing month over month, and query performance on it steadily degrades. PostgreSQL's MVCC model means a `DELETE` doesn't actually remove a row immediately — it marks the old row version as dead, and only `VACUUM` reclaims that space. If `autovacuum` isn't keeping up with the write/delete rate, dead rows accumulate faster than they're cleaned, a state called **table bloat**.

### Tuning Autovacuum for a High-Churn Table

The default autovacuum settings are tuned conservatively for small, low-traffic tables — a high-churn table like `sessions` often needs a per-table override:

```sql
ALTER TABLE sessions SET (
  autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.05,   -- default is 0.2 (20% dead rows before vacuum triggers)
  autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 2,        -- default 2ms; lower runs vacuum more aggressively
  autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.02
);
```

`autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.05` means autovacuum triggers once 5% of the table's rows are dead, instead of waiting for 20% — on a table with millions of rows and constant deletes, the default threshold lets a huge number of dead rows pile up before cleanup even starts.

### Checking Bloat Directly

```sql
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,
       round(n_dead_tup::numeric / NULLIF(n_live_tup + n_dead_tup, 0) * 100, 1) AS dead_pct
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE n_dead_tup > 0
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

A `dead_pct` consistently climbing above 10-20% on a hot table is a clear signal that autovacuum's default thresholds aren't keeping pace with that table's specific write pattern, and it's a candidate for the per-table tuning above.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: Table bloat directly undermines the covering-index and index-only-scan work from Lesson 1.3 — an index-only scan still has to consult the visibility map, and a bloated table with a stale visibility map forces PostgreSQL to fall back to checking the heap anyway, silently erasing the benefit of the optimization.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.4: Knowledge Check — Indexing & Query Tuning
lessons.body:
**Question 1:** Why does a B-Tree index on a JSONB column fail to help a query using the `@>` containment operator?

A) B-Tree indexes only work on text columns
B) B-Tree supports equality and ordering, but not containment — the query needs an operator class the B-Tree structure doesn't implement, so the planner can't use it regardless of tuning
C) JSONB columns can never be indexed
D) The query needs to be rewritten in a different language

**Correct answer: B.** Each index type implements a specific set of operators (its "operator class"). A B-Tree index simply has no code path for evaluating `@>` containment — GIN does, which is why GIN is the correct choice for JSONB/full-text queries.

---

**Question 2:** In an `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` plan, what does `Buffers: shared read=8841` (as opposed to `shared hit`) indicate?

A) 8,841 rows were returned by the query
B) 8,841 blocks were read from disk rather than served from PostgreSQL's shared buffer cache — a strong signal of either a cold cache or a missing index forcing a large scan
C) The query used 8,841 different indexes
D) It's a count of how many times autovacuum has run on this table

**Correct answer: B.** `hit` means the block was already in memory; `read` means PostgreSQL had to fetch it from disk. A plan dominated by `read` on a query you expect to be fast points to either memory pressure or a scan that's touching far more data than necessary.

---

**Question 3:** Why can `pool_mode = transaction` in PgBouncer break code that relies on session-level PostgreSQL features like `LISTEN/NOTIFY` or session advisory locks?

A) PgBouncer doesn't support those features in any mode
B) Under transaction pooling, a client's underlying backend connection is only held for a single transaction and can change between transactions — so state tied to "this specific connection" doesn't persist the way the application might assume
C) Those features were removed in modern PostgreSQL versions
D) It only affects read replicas, never the primary

**Correct answer: B.** Transaction pooling maximizes connection reuse by releasing the backend connection as soon as a transaction ends — which is exactly what breaks any feature whose correctness depends on staying on the same physical connection across multiple transactions.
